source: Ferré (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: MADIL v3.5 learns an input model and an output model as patterns, and picks the pair that compresses the examples best. Search is Monte Carlo tree search guided by description length.
numbers: Public evaluation: found a fit to all training examples on 69 of 400 tasks; 57 correct on all test inputs (82% generalization rate); 2 more correct with one training example misunderstood. Score at ArcPrize 2024 about 7% (private).
limits: Fit is not proof. 12 of 69 fits failed on test. Score table in the PDF text is garbled; only the 7% private figure and the counts above are confirmed.
agent_relevance: Shortest-fit rule is a good filter but must still be checked on held-out cases (G3).

source: Ferré (2025) MADIL, section 8.1 model size
finding: Correct models are large for brute force but short for MDL search. Size counts values, references, functions, patterns, unknowns.
numbers: Correct solutions: size 3 to 46, mean 15.2. Only 4 tasks have a correct solution of size 4 or less. Brute-force DSL search is limited to depth 3-4.
quote: This demonstrates the relevance of description lengths to guide the search.
limits: Size is in the author's own DSL units, not bits of a universal code.
agent_relevance: Description length is useful as a search guide, not only as a final tie-break (S2 and S7).

source: Ferré (2025) MADIL, section 8.2 search efficiency
finding: Greedy MDL search almost always finds the answer when one exists; extra search rarely helps.
numbers: 54 of 69 solutions found on the first greedy rollout. 80% of solutions found in the first 20 s of a 180 s budget. Mean visited models 177 (all tasks), 45 (solved tasks). Best model mean rank 1.6, depth 17 (all) vs 11 (solved).
quote: 54/69 solutions are found on the first MCTS rollout, i.e. with greedy search.
limits: Unsolved tasks build deeper, more complex models: depth rises when nothing fits.
agent_relevance: Rising model complexity without a fit is a signal to stop and switch strategy (S2/S7).

source: Ferré (2025) MADIL, section 8.3 ablations
finding: Most knobs matter little. Strong effects only for sampling a single grid description and for tiny expressions.
numbers: Of 71 tasks solved by some v3.2-v3.6: one description sample (Np=1) loses 19 tasks; expression size Se=1 loses 27; top-1 example description loses 6; no rehearsal factor loses 6; greedy search loses 4; one transition per step loses 3; no test-input check or pruning loses 6. Np=10 vs 100 loses 1; Se=5 vs 9 loses 0.
limits: Task sample is the 71 already-solvable tasks, so it measures loss of search effort, not new gains.
agent_relevance: Several candidate descriptions of the data beat one; keep more than one reading of the examples.

source: Ferré (2025) MADIL, section 8.4 failure analysis
finding: Failures split into wrong-but-fitting programs, missed solutions, and missing primitives.
numbers: 21 training tasks: solution found but wrong on test (cause: contrived expressions that compensate for wrong grid decomposition; worse with fewer examples and larger Se). 62 tasks: solvable but not found; 21 need non-compressive intermediate steps, 15 lack diverse top descriptions, 13 other.
quote: Adding more primitives is unlikely to solve ARC, or may result in ad-hoc solutions.
limits: Author's own diagnosis, no external replication.
agent_relevance: Matches our wrong-but-fitting problem. Pure greedy compression has a local-minimum failure: sometimes the right path first gets longer.

source: Ferré (2025) MADIL vs Icecuber overlap
finding: MDL synthesis and brute-force DSL search solve partly different tasks.
numbers: Evaluation set, all test grids correct: MADIL 59, Icecuber 117 (rerun by author). Overlap 43; 16 solved only by MADIL.
limits: Icecuber rerun by the author; MADIL counts 59 here vs 57 in the other measure (different success rule).
agent_relevance: Different solver families are complementary; an ensemble gains more than tuning one.

source: Ferré (2025) MADIL, conclusion on limits
finding: Author lists structural limits: combinatorial decompositions, input and output models learned separately, no conditional models, hard sequence matching, no part constraints.
numbers: No counts given for this list.
limits: Perspective section, untested claims.
agent_relevance: Learning input and output separately misses input-output links; our agent should look at both together.

source: Ferré (2021) First Steps of an Approach to the ARC Challenge based on Descriptive Grid Models and MDL
finding: Earliest MDL-on-ARC system by the same author; over one year of versions, solved training tasks rose from 5 to 29 of 400 (7.25%) with 30 s per task.
numbers: 29/400 training tasks and 6/400 evaluation tasks (1.5%). For comparison it cites a prior search method at 3% on Kaggle tasks and 7.68% on training. Winner of the 2020 Kaggle ran 20% on its 100 private tasks.
limits: Small numbers; design looked at only a few training tasks first. Grew by hand-added models.
agent_relevance: Shows the MDL route improved about 5 times with better models, not with more compute.

source: Ferré (2021) First Steps, version 1 spurious fits
finding: Early version already showed fit-without-generalization: it explained all training examples on 3 extra tasks but failed their tests.
numbers: v1 solved 3.5 extra training tasks and explained all train examples of 3 more (a79310a0, bb43febb, 694f12f3, a61f2674 listed) but failed tests, often with implausible expressions.
limits: Anecdotal list of tasks.
agent_relevance: Early evidence for G3: a shorter fit still needs a held-out check.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: A 76K-parameter network with no pretraining, trained only on the target puzzle at test time by minimizing code length of puzzle plus weights, solves part of ARC-AGI-1.
numbers: 2000 steps, about 20 min per puzzle on an RTX 4070: 20% of evaluation puzzles and 34.75% of training puzzles (pass@2). Pass@1: 30.25% training, 18.50% evaluation.
quote: CompressARC ... solves 20% of evaluation puzzles by minimizing the description length (MDL) of the target puzzle purely during inference time.
limits: Scores on public evaluation set; budget differs from the 12 h Kaggle rule; no semi-private test.
agent_relevance: Neural MDL at test time is a second MDL route; it needs no program language but needs GPU minutes per item.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC, compute scaling
finding: Accuracy climbs with inference steps and flattens; more guesses help a lot.
limits: Pass@1000 is not a valid benchmark score; it only shows the answer is often in the sample.
agent_relevance: The right answer is often among samples; selecting by shortest code could rank them (S7).

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC baselines
finding: A standard U-Net given the same single-puzzle training does far worse than the MDL network.
numbers: U-Net baseline trained on the target puzzle only: 0.75% on public eval (table text garbled; read as 0.75% for U-Net vs 20% for CompressARC). Random augmentation hurt the U-Net on the training set: 2.5% without vs 1% with.
limits: Table columns misaligned in text extraction; mapping of rows to numbers is my reading.
agent_relevance: The gain comes from the description-length objective, not just test-time fitting.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC, appendix H limits
finding: Abilities CompressARC cannot perform.
numbers: Cannot: map two colors to each other, repeat an operation in series, count, translate or rotate or reflect or rescale, detect connectivity, plan or simulate an agent, extend patterns over long range.
limits: Listed from observed failures on named puzzles, not measured rates.
agent_relevance: These are the skills where an LLM scaffold with explicit steps could add value over pure compression.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Fine-tuned LLMs doing induction (write a program) and transduction (predict output directly) solve different ARC tasks; combining them beats either in some settings.
numbers: ARC-Potpourri: induction 20k samples majority vote 35.25%; transduction without TTT 39.25%; transduction with TTT 56.75% (avg human 60.2%). ARC-Heavy induction 19.25%, transduction no TTT 37.50%, ensemble no TTT 29.75%, transduction with TTT 43.25%.
limits: Ensemble row did not beat transduction in every setting. Rows are BARC models on the 400 public validation tasks.
agent_relevance: Program-writing needs a checker; predicting directly covers fuzzy perceptual tasks. Both routes in one agent.

source: Li et al. (2024) false positives of program fits
finding: Programs that fit all training pairs sometimes still fail the test input.
numbers: About 9% of fitting programs were false positives (fit train, wrong on test). About half of problems with a false positive still had the majority of probability mass on the right answer, so majority vote removes them.
quote: simple majority vote scheme would squash any false positives
limits: Sampling up to 20k programs; effect depends on budget.
agent_relevance: Pairs fit-checking with voting among fitting programs: a cheap guard against wrong-but-fitting rules.

source: Li et al. (2024) complementarity test
finding: Tested whether induction and transduction differ only by random noise. They do not: the tasks each solves are stable across random seeds.
numbers: Two models trained from different initializations solve mostly the same set of problems within each approach (Figure 5B); across approaches the solved sets differ.
limits: Stated via figures; exact overlap counts not in extracted text.
agent_relevance: Supports an ensemble design rather than a single method.

source: Akyürek et al. (2025) Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training
finding: Test-time training of an 8B LM on a task's examples reaches 53.0% on public ARC validation, 61.9% when ensembled with program synthesis (BARC).
numbers: Ablations on a task subset: removing transformations drops 16 tasks (55%); another removal drops 11 (38%); adding loss on demonstration outputs raises 26% to 29%. Table rows seen: 58.5% BARC alone, 62.8% BARC plus TTT.
limits: Row numbers from extracted table, partly garbled; ablations use a subset.
agent_relevance: Test-time learning plus program synthesis is the best-known mix; MDL fit is a candidate ranker.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 Technical Report
finding: Competition review: top private scores rose from 33% to 55.5%; all top entries combine transduction and induction.
numbers: Private eval: ARChitects 53.5%, Barbadillo 40%, alijs 40%; MindsAI 55.5% (not eligible). Best transduction-only and induction-only single entries about 40%. Kaggle 2020 Icecuber 20%; all 2020 entries together solved 49% of private eval. Greenblatt 42-43%.
limits: Report does not mention MADIL or MDL in the extracted text (no match).
agent_relevance: Pure program search tops out near 40% single, so plain MDL/search needs a partner.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 report, brute-force ceiling
finding: Brute-force program search in a DSL can solve about half of ARC-AGI-1 private tasks when entries are pooled, which the organizers read as a sign the benchmark is partly shallow.
numbers: Best single brute-force Kaggle submission 40% private (alijs). Pooled 2020 entries 49%.
quote: a large fraction of the ARC-AGI-1 dataset is overly susceptible to these kinds of brute-force program search techniques
limits: Organizers' interpretation.
agent_relevance: MDL synthesis at 7% is far below search in a large DSL; its value is efficiency and legibility.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC-AGI-2
finding: ARC-AGI-2 was designed to resist brute-force program search; old search methods collapse on it.
numbers: Semi-private (ARC-AGI-1 / ARC-AGI-2): Icecuber 17.0% / 1.6%; ARChitects 56.0% / 2.5%; o3 medium 53.0% / 3.0%; Claude 3.7 (8K) 21.2% / 0.9%. Humans: 75% of attempts by task; every task solved by at least two testers.
limits: Scores dated 14 May 2025.
agent_relevance: A synthesis route tuned to ARC-AGI-1 may not carry over; test on harder items.

source: Hodel (2024) Addressing ARC via Procedural Example Generation (RE-ARC)
finding: Provides generators for ARC tasks plus a DSL used by many entries; only the opening was read this session.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not read beyond the first page.
agent_relevance: Useful data source for DSL-based synthesis.

source: Ferré (2025) ARC-MDL GitHub repository README
finding: Open OCaml code for MADIL; README gives no scores and lists no limitations.
numbers: 730 commits, GPL-3.0; cites tech report arXiv:2112.00848; says best approaches solve about 20% of tasks, humans about 80%.
limits: Fetched via a summarizing tool, not raw page text. Nothing was re-run by us.
agent_relevance: Code exists to check the 7% and ablation claims.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder
finding: Wake-sleep Bayesian program learning that grows a library of abstractions that compress programs; MADIL cites it as related.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Only header read; not an ARC result.
agent_relevance: Library learning is the piece MADIL names as future work.

source: Cross-source note: no independent replication of MADIL
finding: No other group's re-run of MADIL was found in the sources opened. All MADIL numbers are the single author's. ArcPrize 2025 and later reports were not searched (web search quota was exhausted).
numbers: 0 replications found among 10 opened sources.
limits: Absence in a quota-limited search is weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Treat the 82% generalization and 80%-in-20-s figures as single-lab.

source: Cross-source note: MDL versus LLM ensembles on ARC
finding: MADIL about 7% private; CompressARC 20% (pass@2, public eval); Icecuber 17% on ARC-AGI-1 semi-private; fine-tuned LLM transduction/induction ensembles 53-62%. No opened source puts MDL selection inside an LLM loop at matched cost.
numbers: MADIL ~7%, CompressARC 20%, Icecuber 17-20%, BARC+TTT ensemble 61.9%.
limits: Different splits (private, semi-private, public) and compute budgets, so not strictly comparable.
agent_relevance: MDL-style ranking inside an LLM loop is untested but cheap, for S7.
